name: Berber ahidus and ahwash (Atlas Mountains)
lineage: Berber (Imazighen / Amazigh) collective song-and-dance tradition of the Atlas Mountain ranges across Morocco, with ahidus the central-and-northern Middle-Atlas form (Tamazight-speaking populations) and ahwash the Souss-region southern-Atlas form (Tashelhiyt-speaking populations). Performance involves two facing rows of dancers (mixed men and women in ahidus, often single-sex in ahwash) executing synchronized arm-and-shoulder choreography while singing antiphonal call-and-response over bendir frame-drum accompaniment, with the amdyaz (poet-leader) improvising the opening verse-line that the chorus answers in unison. Modal vocabulary draws on regional pentatonic frameworks with characteristic Atlas-region melodic-contour conventions. The amzwaj poetic-form (couplet-and-response architecture) governs verse structure, with seasonal-and-occasional repertoires for harvest, wedding, and tribal-assembly contexts. Miriam Rovsing Olsen's 1990s Atlas fieldwork (published as Chants et danses de l'Atlas, Actes Sud / Cité de la musique 1997, with Ocora-Radio France C 559035 companion recordings) is the principal scholarly documentation. Distinguished from Berber Rif and Kabyle vocal traditions by Atlas-region poly-strophic verse structure and bendir-frame-drum-dominant percussion; distinguished from Andalusi-Maghrebi nuba by Tamazight-language and outdoor-village (not court-and-chamber) performance context; distinguished from Tuareg by sedentary-village (not nomadic-pastoral) base and bendir (vs tendé pestle-drum) percussion.
